tagline.text: Mindanao's largest and safest city, filled with the scent of durian

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (low typhoon impact), August Kadayawan Festival

image.credit: Aimee Valencia / CC BY 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: Mindanao's largest city, known for strict ordinances that keep it clean and safe. With the Philippine Eagle Center and Eden Nature Park, a paradise of tropical fruit led by durian, and the
August
Kadayawan Festival, there's plenty to enjoy, and it's the gateway to Samal Island and Mount Apo.
Davao City sits on Davao Gulf in southeastern Mindanao, Mindanao's largest city and, with a population of about 1.8 million, the economic center of the southern Philippines. Covering over
², it's one of the largest cities by area in the Philippines — the country's highest peak, Mount Apo (about
), rises behind downtown, and Samal Island floats offshore. The sea, the mountains, and the city are all within an hour of each other.

Davao is famous across the Philippines as "a city where the rules are followed." Long-standing strict ordinances ban smoking in public places, prohibit firecrackers, enforce speed limits downtown, and restrict late-night alcohol sales; the streets stay clean, and taxi drivers generally run their meters honestly. It's the most comfortable city to start from for anyone visiting Mindanao for the first time.

The city has another side too — "the fruit basket of the Philippines." Surrounding farms produce durian, marang, mangosteen, pomelo, rambutan, and bananas in abundance, and fresh tropical fruit is cheap and easy to find at stalls across the city. Durian in particular is Davao's symbol, appearing everywhere from a monument outside the airport to ice cream, candy, and cakes. Every third week of
August
, the Kadayawan Festival celebrates the harvest, filling the city with parades of flower-decked floats and traditional indigenous costumes.

The mountains around Davao are home to several indigenous groups, including the Bagobo, Manobo, and Matigsalug, bringing a range of traditions into the city's culture. Nature spots like the Philippine Eagle Center, where you can see the endangered Philippine eagle up close, and Eden Nature Park on a highland plateau at about
, are also within
1 hour
of downtown. It suits family travelers, food and fruit lovers, and anyone using the city as a base for a Samal Island getaway or a Mount Apo climb.
A conservation and breeding facility in Calinan, Malagos, where you can see one of the world's largest eagles up close — the Philippine eagle, the national bird. It's about
1 hour
from downtown by car, and the birds are most active in the morning.

blocks.title: Malagos Garden Resort and chocolate experience

children.text: A garden-style resort right next to the eagle center, with bird shows and a butterfly garden. Malagos chocolate, made from Davao-grown cacao, has won international awards for its quality and makes a popular souvenir.
A nature park on a mountain in Toril at about
elevation, with a pine forest, flower gardens, and activities like ziplining and a sky cycle. Enjoying a buffet lunch in the cool air is a popular way to spend the visit.

You can pick out seasonal durian, marang, and mangosteen and eat them on the spot at the fruit stalls in front of People's Park or at the Bankerohan market. If it's your first durian, it's worth asking for a sweeter variety.

blocks.title: People's Park and San Pedro Cathedral

children.text: A downtown park with sculptures depicting indigenous tribes and a large durian-shaped dome. Nearby San Pedro Cathedral is Davao's oldest church, notable for its striking, ship-shaped modern building.
In the evening, stalls line Roxas Avenue selling barbecue, grilled seafood, and cheap clothes and goods. It's a good place to experience locals' evening culture.

blocks.title: Jack's Ridge views and night scenery

children.text: A cluster of view restaurants on a hill west of downtown, with sweeping views of the city, Davao Gulf, and Samal Island at night. It's also a historic site, once home to a Japanese army headquarters during the Pacific War.

Fresh tuna caught in Davao Gulf and from General Santos further south is the heart of Davao's food scene, served as grilled tuna jaw, tuna sashimi, and kinilaw. Coastal restaurants serve it all cheaply.
Arrive at Davao Airport, check in downtown, then stroll through People's Park and San Pedro Cathedral.
Have lunch of grilled tuna jaw at a tuna specialty restaurant.
Sample durian and tropical fruit at the Magsaysay Park stalls, then browse Mindanao handicrafts at Aldevinco Shopping Center.
Watch the sunset and city lights from Jack's Ridge over dinner, then stroll through the Roxas night market.
Head to Calinan Malagos to visit the Philippine Eagle Center and Malagos Garden Resort.
Have lunch in Malagos and buy chocolate souvenirs.
Head to Eden Nature Park in Toril for a garden walk and zipline, or return downtown to relax at the malls and cafes.
Enjoy a beach getaway on Samal Island, about
15 minutes
away by boat, or head off for a Mount Apo climb.
Learn about Davao's indigenous tribes and the city's history at Museo Dabawenyo in the Poblacion.
Stop by San Pedro Cathedral, then have lunch at a tuna restaurant downtown.
Shop, have coffee, and enjoy durian desserts at SM Lanang Premier in Lanang or Abreeza Mall in Bajada.
The Eagle Center and Eden Nature Park on the outskirts have slippery roads and awkward viewing in the rain, so it's better to postpone them to a clear day.

A long-distance ferry runs from Manila to Davao, but it takes 2–3 days, so travelers rarely use it. For Samal Island, take a ferry or roll-on/roll-off boat from Sasa wharf or a downtown pier.
Davao taxis have a low flag-down rate and the meter is generally used properly. Grab is also widely used, and jeepneys have a base fare of about
. If you're covering outlying attractions such as the Eagle Center and Eden Nature Park in a day, it's convenient to charter a taxi or van for the day (about

Davao lies south of the Philippines' main typhoon path, so typhoon damage is very rare. There's no clear division between dry and wet seasons — rain falls fairly evenly year-round — and temperatures stay around 23–33 degrees all year. Any time of year is fine to visit, but
January
to
May
, with comparatively more clear days, is the most pleasant. From
June
to
November
, afternoon showers are frequent, so it's best to schedule outlying trips in the morning.
The biggest event is the Kadayawan Festival, centered on the third week of
August

each year, with floats decorated in flowers and fruit, indigenous tribal dance competitions, and street performances — and it's also when durian and other fruit are at their most abundant. Durian season runs roughly from
August
to
October
, when it's cheapest and best. Accommodation fills up fast during the festival, so book one to two months ahead.

Accommodation splits roughly into three areas. Lanang, near the airport, has malls, upscale hotels, and residences, convenient for family travelers. The downtown Poblacion and C.M. Recto Street area is walkable and close to sights like People's Park and the Roxas night market. Budget guesthouses and business hotels run about
a night, mid-range hotels about
, and upscale hotels
and up. If you'd rather look out at the sea, staying at a Samal Island resort and commuting by boat to downtown is another option.

Food is central to a Davao trip. Beyond durian, you can easily find soft-fleshed marang, sweet-tart mangosteen, and large pomelo at markets and stalls. If durian feels intimidating, durian ice cream, candy, or cheesecake are a gentler introduction. The long-running local cafe Lachi's is famous for its durian desserts, and Penong's, a chain that started in Davao, is a budget favorite for charcoal barbecue and rice. Coastal tuna restaurants let you enjoy grilled tuna jaw, tuna sinigang, and tuna kinilaw all at once. There are also several Korean restaurants and grocery stores downtown, so long-term residents have little trouble.

Davao is a city with a total public smoking ban. Smoking is prohibited on the street, in parks, and in most restaurants both indoors and out, including e-cigarettes — you may only smoke in designated smoking areas.
Many hotels, malls, and taxis ban bringing durian inside. Eat durian on the spot at the stall, and if you want to take some with you, buy a sealed processed product instead.
Davao taxis are generally honest, but it's still a good habit to check that the meter is running when you board. Using Grab is convenient since the fare is set in advance.

The Philippine Eagle Center and Eden Nature Park are in different directions, so visiting both in one day means a lot of travel. It's more relaxed to split them across two days — one for Malagos, one for Eden and downtown.
Fruit prices drop sharply during durian season (August–
October
). Stalls often sell by weight, so it's worth asking the price before choosing.
ATMs are plentiful around the malls and downtown, and card payment works well. Fruit stalls and the night market, however, take cash only.
Most public buildings and mall entrances do a bag check. It goes quickly if you cooperate, so there's no need to feel uneasy about it.
Davao City ordinances strictly enforce rules on smoking, firecrackers, speeding, and late-night alcohol sales. Travelers aren't exempt, and violations can bring heavy fines or detention.

Davao City itself is relatively safe, but travel advisories are in effect for parts of Mindanao. Check your home country's latest travel advisory before you go, and travel to the city's outskirts during daylight hours.
Watch out for phone and wallet pickpocketing in the night market and busy markets.
Durian is locally believed to be a "heaty" fruit, and there's a local saying against eating too much of it with alcohol. Anyone with a sensitive stomach should try just a little at first.
Low-lying roads can flood during heavy wet-season rain, so leave plenty of time for getting to the airport.
In Davao, even a single instance of smoking on the street can bring a fine or detention. If you smoke, be sure to find a designated smoking area.
